lines: Here are six real events: a few clicks, one scroll, and one record where a field that's usually a number shows up as a string instead.
Four different shapes, one outright type conflict. This is what semi-structured data actually looks like once it leaves a toy example.
The question this topic answers is simple: what do you store this in, so that nothing gets lost and nothing gets slow?
Suppose you pick one fixed struct: a string column for event type, an int thirty-two column for button ID. That's the shape most of these six records share.
Can that one struct hold every one of the six records, without quietly throwing anything away?
answer: No. A null can stand in for a field that's simply missing, but it can't stand in for a field the struct never had a column for, or a value whose type the column can't represent at all.
Watch what happens to the scroll event, and to the one record where button ID shows up as text.

lines: Force all six records into that struct, and the scroll event's only real field, depth percent, has nowhere to go — there's no column for it.
Worse, the record where button ID is the string "unknown" doesn't even get left null. The struct's int thirty-two column simply can't hold it, so it's silently dropped.
Three of the six records lose real data. Nothing in the struct itself tells you that happened.
Now the alternative: the Variant binary encoding. A metadata dictionary holding every field name once, plus a per-record value that can be any shape at all.
This topic builds that encoder by hand, straight from the specification's own byte layout — the header byte, the dictionary offsets, the value's type tag.
Decode every one of the six records back, and every single one matches the original exactly. Nothing silently dropped, because nothing required a fixed schema in the first place.
Now a different question. Say you want every event where event type equals "click". Does answering that mean decoding the entire Variant binary value for all six records?
answer: Not necessarily. If event type is shredded into its own typed Parquet column, a reader can filter on that column directly, the exact same way it filters any ordinary column — no Variant decoding required.
The catch is that shredding only works field by field, and only when a field's actual type cooperates.

lines: Shred event type and button ID into typed columns, field by field, following the specification's own rules for the value and its shredded counterpart.
Three records shred completely, with nothing left over. Two keep a real residual field — the scroll event's depth percent, and the one extra label field.
And one falls back entirely: button ID as the string "unknown" can't go in an int thirty-two column, so it stays in the residual value, exactly as the spec requires.
Here's the payoff. Event type happens to be a string in every one of these six records, so it's shredded every single time, with nothing left over for that field.
Finding the five click events means reading the typed event type column alone — zero bytes of the residual Variant value get touched at all.
Measured in bytes: two hundred fifty as plain JSON strings, one hundred fifty-five as an unshredded Variant, one hundred twenty-six once event type and button ID are shredded.
Shredding wins on size here, but only modestly — a fairer comparison needs a bigger dataset to really separate these numbers.
That modest size gain isn't really the point. The point is the filter from two steps ago: zero residual bytes read for a typed column's own query.
Shredding earns its keep mostly through pushdown and statistics, the same tools row-group and page skipping use — not mainly through smaller files.
Step back, and the shape of the lesson is the same one this whole chapter keeps returning to: a fixed schema is fast but brittle, and it drops what it wasn't built for.
A Variant keeps everything, typed or not, at the cost of being opaque until decoded. Shredding is the compromise — typed speed for the fields that earn it, a residual for the rest.
The rule that makes it safe: shred what's genuinely typed, and never force a schema that quietly throws real data away.
